persnickety

per-SNIK-uh-tee · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Persnickety is too concerned about small, unimportant details.

The persnickety librarian insisted every returned book be aligned exactly with the shelf edge, down to the millimeter.

Example

The persnickety editor sent back the article four times over a single misplaced comma, ignoring every larger issue in the draft.

Persnickety describes someone who fusses over small, often unimportant, details -- usually to a degree that seems excessive to everyone else.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

fussy: Fussy means overly particular about small things, and it is the plainest everyday word for it -- a fussy dresser, someone fussy about seating plans. Persnickety means the same kind of fussing with a playful, old-fashioned flavor: the word you choose to tease someone about it rather than to complain.

nitpicky: Nitpicky means finding tiny faults in other people's work -- flagging every comma, every rounding error -- criticism aimed outward. Persnickety fussing usually points at one's own standards and routines, how the pencils are arranged or the books line up, and it carries a lighter, teasing tone.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

easygoing: relaxed about small details

undemanding: not fussy about requirements

Where it sits · how consuming the fussing becomes

particular → persnickety → obsessive

particular vs. persnickety: Someone particular has clear preferences but doesn't fuss endlessly; a persnickety person goes further, dwelling on tiny details until everyone notices.

obsessive vs. persnickety: Someone obsessive over details takes the fussing to an extreme, well past ordinary persnickety behavior.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together: Persnickety's exact origin is genuinely uncertain -- it likely grew out of the older British word "pernickety," itself of unclear Scottish-dialect origin, with no confirmed root that survives elsewhere in English.

Use the root in a new word: pernickety: "Pernickety" is the older British spelling of the same word -- both versions mean exactly the same thing today.
